title: MB5-01423
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, the appellant, an Ivorian citizen, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, the appellant, an Ivorian citizen, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). He is submitting that the RPD erred in its analysis of the internal flight alternative (IFA).

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) allows the appeal, sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, namely, that XXXX XXXX is a refugee under section 96 of the IRPA. III. BACKGROUND A. Summary of alleged facts

In the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), which he signed on November 27, 2014, the appellant states that he agreed to have sexual relations with an Ivorian businessman in exchange for his support in obtaining employment and then financial assistance, particularly in business activities. He adds that their relationship was discovered by a young Muslim, that he was then sought by members of a Muslim youth association and that on the night of XXXX XXXX to XXXX, 2014, his warehouse where he kept his products was ransacked.1
In addition to his BOC Form, the appellant, then referred to as the claimant, filed documents into evidence before the RPD.2 B. RPD decision
The hearing before the RPD was held on February 17, 2015, and the decision to reject the claim for refugee protection was rendered on March 4, 2015.3
In its reasons for decision, the RPD found the claimant to be credible, and the only determinative issue was the IFA.4
The cities of Korhogo and Boundiali, located in Côte d'Ivoire's north, were proposed as an IFA on account of their distance from Abidjan, where the claimant lived.5

In this regard, here is the RPD's analysis: [translation] [12] As far as the first prong is concerned, when questioned about his ability to relocate to the areas proposed by the panel, at first the claimant simply replied that the members of the Association des jeunes musulmans (AJMI) [association of Muslim youth] who suspect him and accuse him of being a homosexual will find him no matter where he goes in the country. After questions from his lawyer, the claimant eventually added that the AJCMI is present in all the cities of Côte d'Ivoire. [13] The panel finds the simple allegation that the AJCMI is present in all the cities of Côte d'Ivoire to be quite simply too vague to conclude that this association has the means of finding the claimant no matter where he goes in the country. In fact, in reply to the panel's many questions on the methods that the AJCMI would use to track him down, when this association did not manage to do so in over seven months while he was living in Grand-Bassam, the claimant simply repeated that sooner or later, his persecuting agent would be able to track him down, without providing further details. [14] It must be recalled that it is up to the claimant to provide satisfactory evidence that the AJCMI has the power and resources necessary to find him. Thus, absent this information, simply alleging that the association is present throughout the country does not, in and of itself, establish on a balance of probabilities that the claimant runs a serious risk of persecution throughout his country. Furthermore, the claimant failed to show, either by his testimony or the evidence on the record, that the authorities are aware of the accusations against him and are in close pursuit. [15] It must also be recalled that according to the claimant's testimony, he is heterosexual. He is not homosexual. He engaged in this practice solely in response to an economic need. Accordingly, it is the panel's opinion that his way of life in Korhogo or Boundiali would not draw the malevolent attention of homophobic groups. [16] The panel points out that it took account of the fact that the claimant lived in hiding in Grand-Bassam for over seven months. The fact remains, though, that he continued visiting his mother without being located by his supposed agents of persecution.6

As for the second prong of the IFA analysis, the RPD found that it was not unreasonable for the claimant, XXXX years old, resourceful and well versed in agricultural trade, to move to Korhogo or Boundiali.7

Hence its conclusion: [translation] [18] Having considered all the evidence, the panel finds that the claimant did not discharge his burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility of persecution on one of the Convention grounds or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, or a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to his country.8 C. Grounds of appeal and decision sought
In his memorandum, the appellant submits that the RPD erred in its analysis.9

First, he points out that the RPD found his testimony to be credible. He claims to have been persecuted because he was accused of being homosexual by the members of his Muslim community. And in his BOC Form, he states that should he return home, he would be persecuted because the authorities abuse, harass, humiliate and jail homosexuals.10

He then submits that the documentary evidence confirms that the treatment afforded sexual minorities is the same throughout Côte d'Ivoire: they are rejected and hunted down despite homosexuality not being a crime as such. He adds that sections of the Code pénal [penal code] describe the homosexual act as constituting public indecency and that, what is more, the practice of homosexuality is considered against Islamic morals.11
He further submits that in light of his testimony and the documentary evidence, it is unreasonable to find there to be an IFA in two cities in the country's north, a mostly Muslim region.12

Last, he submits that the RPD cannot, on the one hand, find his testimony as a whole to be credible while, on the other hand, reject a portion of it, namely the part about the ability of the Association des jeunes musulmans de la Côte d'Ivoire (l'AJMCI) [association of Muslim youth of Côte d'Ivoire] to find him wherever he goes in the country.13
The appellant requests that the RAD set aside the RPD's determination and allow his claim for refugee protection or refer the matter to the RPD for a new hearing.14

A statement signed by his lawyer indicates that the appellant is not presenting any evidence as referred to in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA or requesting a hearing before the RAD.15 IV. APPROACH TO BE TAKEN IN THIS APPEAL A. The appellant's position

In his memorandum, the appellant submits that there is no reason for the RAD to show deference to the RPD for any error of law and fact, as is the case in the case at hand. He adds that the RAD must conduct an independent assessment of all the evidence in order to correct any error of the RPD in the findings of fact or the assessment of the law with respect to the facts.16 B. Brief summary of certain Federal Court decisions

In Huruglica, Justice Phelan finds that the RAD must conduct an independent assessment of the refugee protection claim in order to arrive at its own opinion and that it is not necessary, in order to trigger this remedial power, that the RAD find error on the part of the RPD on some standard of review basis.17

In Kurtzmalaj, the Honourable Justice Gagné determines that for IFA findings, the RAD owes no deference to the RPD, and it is necessary for it to review the relevant evidence and to formulate its own opinion.18 In Brodrick, in which the RAD confirmed the RPD's decision that she had an IFA, the Honourable Justice Diner determines that, in this case, the RAD should have undertaken its own review of the documentary evidence.19 C. An independent review of the relevant evidence

Drawing as much as possible on the Federal Court decisions rendered to date, I am of the opinion that, in this case, I must assess all the relevant evidence and arrive at my own conclusions regarding the IFA.

I have concluded that, in light of the documentary evidence and considering the personal situation of the appellant, who was found to be credible by the RPD, there is no IFA available to the appellant in Korhogo or Boundiali. Here is why.
paragraphs.heading_before: V. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: According to the documentary evidence, although homosexuality is not formally outlawed in Côte d'Ivoire, the fact that certain sections of the Code pénal make reference to it could lead law enforcement to round them up in inappropriate cases. In addition, there is homophobia in Côte d'Ivoire, and members of sexual minorities must conceal their sexual orientation to avoid being the target of profanity, humiliation, discrimination and violence. While the documentary evidence indicates that members of sexual minorities may be better accepted in urban areas, it should be pointed out that they are stigmatized and at times assaulted in parts of Abidjan, and frequently the target of violence.20
paragraphs.heading_before: A. Information contained in the documentary evidence

paragraphs.text: Following a mission in Côte d'Ivoire from November 26 to December 7, 2012, the Office français de protection des réfugiés et apatrides (OFPRA) [French office for the protection of refugees and stateless persons] published a report containing fairly precise and detailed information on the situation of homosexuals in this country. The report indicates that the violence and abuse committed against homosexuals can come from both the population and law enforcement, and it describes an extremely violent assault committed against a young homosexual while the authorities stood idly by. The report goes on to state that homosexuals dare not file complaints out of fear of family violence and that the problems they encounter are generally denied by the government.21

The Report of the Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review dealing with Côte d'Ivoire underscores the fact that the Ivorian authorities did not accept two recommendations, one by the Netherlands and the other by Slovenia, calling for measures to prevent discrimination based on gender and sexual orientation and for specific awareness campaigns to help sensitize the Ivorian general public to the rights of lesbian, homosexual, bisexual, transgender and inter-sexed individuals.22 B. Appellant's fear of persecution

In the case at hand, the RPD found the appellant's testimony to be credible. The appellant stated that the homosexual relationship he had with a businessman was discovered by a young Muslim and that he was then sought by members of a Muslim youth association who, in all likelihood, were the ones who ransacked his warehouse in March 2014. That the appellant does not define his sexual orientation as homosexual in no way limits his testimony-found credible-that members of a Muslim youth association have it in for him because he had homosexual relations which they condemn. What matters is that he fears being persecuted because he has been reproached for these activities.

Although refugee protection claimants must establish their claim on a balance of probabilities, they do not, however, have to prove that persecution would be more likely than not. In other words, the evidence must not necessarily show that a claimant has suffered or will suffer persecution. Indeed, as I understand the case law in that regard, what the evidence must establish is that the refugee protection claimant has a well-founded fear of persecution on one of the grounds set out in the IRPA.23 Moreover, in order to conclude that there is a reasonable fear of persecution or, in other words, a reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution, there need not be more than a 50% chance (i.e., a probability), but there must be more than a minimal possibility,24 given that there is no intermediate ground between the two limits.25

Persecution is generally defined as the serious interference with a basic human right,26 and the word "persecute" means to harass or afflict with repeated acts of cruelty or annoyance; to afflict persistently.27 While it is true that the dividing line between persecution and discrimination or harassment is difficult to establish, the case law indicates that discrimination will only amount to persecution when it is serious or systematic enough to be characterized as persecution.28 In drawing on two decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada, Justice Bédard states that before finding that persecution exists, there is a need to consider whether a basic right was violated and then verify whether the violation was repetitive or systematic.29

In light of the documentary evidence analyzed earlier, it is my opinion that the situation encountered today in Côte d'Ivoire by members of sexual minorities can indeed be characterized as persecution suffered by all of the members of this particular social group.

The RPD found that the appellant was credible, but that an IFA would nonetheless be available to him if he moved to Korhogo or Boundiali, in the northern part of Côte d'Ivoire. Both cities are far closer to the border with Mali than to the Ivorian capital of Yamoussoukro.30

While a refugee protection claimant has the burden of establishing that he has no IFA in another part of the country,31 one must bear in mind that the RPD has an active role to play in determining the facts, in this case having to do with the situation faced by homosexuals or those perceived as such by individuals or groups who discriminate against them or persecute them in Côte d'Ivoire. In fact, as proposed by the UNHCR32 and by the doctrine,33 when conducting the IFA analysis, even though the burden of proof rests on the claimant, the task of establishing all the pertinent facts must be shared between the claimant and the examiner (the RPD in the case at hand).

When examining an IFA, the first question to ask is whether there is another part of the country where the refugee protection claimant would not be subjected to persecution or to a risk to his life.34 In this respect, reputable authors suggest focusing in particular on the question of whether adequate protection on the part of the authorities is available in the proposed locations.35

According to the documentary evidence, the most serious human rights problems plaguing Côte d'Ivoire in recent years were security force abuse and the government's inability to enforce the rule of law. Other findings: the judiciary is underfunded and ineffective; there is a scarcity of trained magistrates and lawyers, particularly outside of major cities; and quite often the tendency is to resort to what is called customary law.36 This information has to do with the general public. In my opinion, taking into account the documentary evidence on the situation of sexual minorities living in Côte d'Ivoire, there is cause to conclude that the appellant cannot expect to receive adequate protection should he move to Korhogo or Boundiali and be faced with threats or aggression on the part of members of a Muslim youth association.

As for the question of whether such an association has the necessary power and resources to track down the appellant if he moved to either of these cities, I find it very plausible that the association does, in fact, have the network it needs to one day identify the appellant. First, it should be pointed out that the appellant is himself a Muslim and that he even belonged to the association in question.37 That being the case, it can be assumed that once settled in Korhogo or Boundiali, he will meet other Muslims and possibly members of this association, which appears to have a national presence. Second, his testimony that members of this association had it in for him because they discovered his homosexual relationship with a businessman was found to be credible by the RPD. Lastly, although I found no information in the documentary evidence on the relationships among members of the same Ivorian religious association, it is reasonable to believe, in my opinion, that these relationships make it easier to transmit information of such a scandalous nature, to their eyes, as forbidden sexual relations on the part of one of their members.

In this context, and having independently reviewed all of the evidence, I find that the appellant would not have an IFA, particularly by moving to Korhogo or Boundiali. Consequently, there is no need for me to analyze the second prong of the IFA.

For these reasons, I set aside the RPD's determination and substitute a determination that, in my opinion, should have been made, namely, that XXXX XXXX is a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA.

The appeal is allowed.
